summary: FLAMEPRINT is a fire-safety intelligence system for crewed space habitats, built for the “Flame in Freefall” challenge. It answers one question: “Is my habitat safe from fire, and how sure are we?” Users pick a habitat (ISS, Moon base, spacesuit, rover, Mars) and see which materials are high risk, which NASA PSI investigations back that up, and an evidence grade (A/B/C/M) showing how much real NASA data supports the answer. For the Moon base it shows that 6 of 8 materials are high risk. The grade is C because PSI has no lunar-gravity fire tests, and the Moon base’s 30% O₂ is above the highest oxygen level in the loaded solid-material tests (22.2%). FLAMEPRINT maps where NASA data ends, recommends the next test (solid materials, 30–100% O₂, lunar gravity, aligned with the planned FM2), and generates a one-page Fire Passport with prevention, detection and suppression guidance. All scores, grades and gaps are computed in code from 862 real PSI test records. AI only words the evidence, and every citation is checked. The principle is simple: untested does not mean safe.
details:
What it does. FLAMEPRINT starts from the mission instead of the database. The user picks a habitat and the system answers on five pages:

  • Answer: a verdict, the evidence grade, a gravity flame visual and the top materials at risk.
  • Evidence: the NASA PSI investigations that back the answer, each ranked on six factors.
  • Gaps: a 2D map and a 3D condition space of oxygen, pressure and airflow, showing where NASA has tested and where it has not, plus the next tests to run.
  • Brief: prevention, detection and suppression guidance with citations.
  • Compare: what changes between two habitats, such as ISS to Moon base, including materials that change risk level and new gaps.

Tools for users and scientists.

  • Can I bring this aboard? checks whether an item is safe to take to a habitat.
  • Data Lab lets users plug in official PSI CSV, XLSX, JSON or PDF files in a structured format and export a model-ready CSV.
  • Ask the Archive is a RAG tool that answers questions about fuels, oxygen levels, suppression, detection and hardware, with cited sources.
  • Investigation tab shows whether each investigation comes from the challenge brief or from other objectives.
  • Fire Passport is a printable one-page summary of a habitat.
  • Down to Earth links the research to Earth uses.

How it works. The backend (FastAPI, Python) loads 24 NASA investigations (22 in PSI, 2 planned), 862 real test records from 10 PSI experimental tables, and 9 NASA reference documents. Ranking, evidence grades and gap detection are deterministic code. The Groq LLM only writes prose from a fixed evidence packet, and each citation is audited. It never produces a number. The app also works with the LLM turned off.

Scientific honesty. No data is invented. Every value is labelled PSI data, approx, unknown, illustrative or modeled. The material-risk model is illustrative, and pressure effects are not yet modeled. The dataset is a selected set of PSI tables, not a complete inventory of NASA fire tests.

Impact and potential. Fire-safety and materials engineers get a traceable evidence trail in every design review. The project is at the pre-pilot stage with no customers or investors claimed. Next steps are more PSI tables and partner datasets, and later sealed Earth systems such as aircraft cabins.

Design. The interface is deep-space navy, iOS-style glassmorphism with solar-yellow accents, a GLSL flame shader, a 3D condition-space explorer, and motion that respects reduced-motion settings.

HOW WE BUILT IT: The idea, the research direction, the design and frontend concept, and the key decisions were created by our team, Peak Hour Pandas, through our own brainstorming and collaboration. We used AI as an assistant to speed up the build. Claude Code (Anthropic) helped us write, debug and test the code and documentation, and the team directed the work, reviewed it and tested the result. Inside the app, Groq (openai/gpt-oss-120b) is used only to word briefs, answer Ask the Archive questions and extract PDF metadata. It never computes scores, grades or gaps; those are deterministic code with audited citations. No NASA logos or branding are used.

Tools used. Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, Framer Motion, React Three Fiber and Three.js with GLSL, FastAPI, Pydantic, optional PostgreSQL with pgvector, Groq API (openai/gpt-oss-120b), pytest and Vitest (55 backend tests, 8 frontend tests), GitHub and Vercel.

Team Peak Hour Pandas: Hamza Safdar, M. Farhan Abid, Armaan Akhtar, Ahmed Mughal, Arham, Zaki Norani.
